READING

**The financial comparison, correctly assembled**

VELLACOTT's net capital requirement is GBP 2,680,000. TARNSIDE's is GBP 1,730,000. The differential is GBP 950,000 in TARNSIDE's favour. Against that, VELLACOTT returns GBP 190,000 a year in fuel savings. Simple payback on the extra outlay: five years. For a year-round licensed operator with no realistic exit from the route, five years is a short planning horizon. Beyond year five VELLACOTT is generating a net return on the additional investment, and it never stops doing so for as long as the Suilvenaig operates.

That arithmetic alone makes VELLACOTT the financially stronger course over any medium or long horizon. But the capital difference is real and deserves acknowledgement: GBP 950,000 is a large sum for an operation of this scale and cannot simply be waved away in favour of the headline payback number.

**The charter risk is more serious than it looks**

TARNSIDE's GBP 310,000 charter is presented as a line item. It is actually the load-bearing pillar of the entire course. Cormorant Sound Ferries holds a year-round licence. You operate one vessel. For twelve weeks beginning 2027-01-05, the Brindlemere is unavailable, and the licensed service is maintained entirely by a vessel you do not own, operated by a third party, agreed only in principle with Sorrelbank Marine. If that charter vessel has a mechanical failure, a crewing problem, or a regulatory issue at any point during those twelve weeks, the service stops. There is no fallback. Eleven crossings a day in May–September, five a day otherwise: even in January the route is live and passengers and vehicles depend on it.

The charter is also only agreed in principle. That is not a contract. Between today and signature there is room for renegotiation, availability problems, or withdrawal. The GBP 310,000 figure could move.

This is the central vulnerability of TARNSIDE and it tends to be underweighted because it is expressed as a cost rather than a risk.

**The hull is not a detail**

A re-engined Brindlemere is a 1995 hull with new engines. The March 2026 survey found no steelwork required, which is genuinely good news, but that survey is now six months old and the vessel is now thirty-one years old. Future surveys will not necessarily be as clean. Plating, framing, and structural members age regardless of what is put in the engine room. By the time TARNSIDE's engines have completed their working life and another decision is required, the hull will be approaching forty. VELLACOTT replaces a thirty-one-year-old hull with a nine-year-old hull. The value of that difference compounds over time in the form of lower maintenance spend, less survey risk, lower likelihood of unplanned out-of-service periods, and a better residual value if the vessel is ever sold.

**The masters problem is real but bounded**

Losing two of nine masters to retirement is not trivial. Going from nine to seven reduces the rota by roughly twenty-two percent, and the seven remaining all need a six-week endorsement course before they can operate the Suilvenaig. That training must be staggered—you cannot take all seven off the rota at once—and you will need at minimum one endorsed master available from the date of handover in November 2026.

The practical path: identify whether any of the seven are willing and available to attend the course immediately, engage with the training provider now, and consider whether an endorsed master can be brought in on a short-term contract to cover the gap period. If necessary, recruit to replace the two retiring masters with candidates who already hold the endorsement. None of this is comfortable or cheap, but none of it is an operational ceiling. It is a management task with a foreseeable end point. The rota at seven experienced masters is tighter but operable for a single-vessel route on known crossing times.

By contrast, TARNSIDE's master problem is zero: it keeps all nine, requires no training, and has no recruitment exposure. That is a genuine advantage and should not be ignored.

**The insurance gap**

No quote exists for the Suilvenaig. This is a material unknown. A 2017 vessel should, in general, attract equal or better terms than a re-engined 1995 vessel, but there is no guarantee, and the broker's silence so far is a gap that needs closing before commitment. If the Suilvenaig insurance premium is significantly higher than current terms, it will erode the fuel saving and extend the payback period. This must be resolved as a condition of proceeding with VELLACOTT, not after.

The Kittiwake valuation holds until 2027-02-11. The Suilvenaig is available from 2026-11-20. There is a window of roughly two and a half months during which an insurance quote can be obtained, the endorsement training can be initiated, the linkspan contract can be let, and the Brindlemere can be sold within the holding period. Tight but workable.

**Timing and sequencing**

Under VELLACOTT, taking handover in November 2026 means the Suilvenaig enters service before the 2027 summer season. Training, linkspan works, and Brindlemere disposal can all run in parallel through the winter. There is no gap in licensed service.

Under TARNSIDE, the yard period runs from 2027-01-05 for twelve weeks, finishing approximately late March 2027. This is in the winter timetable (five crossings a day), which is the best possible time for a planned absence—but only if the charter holds and the vessel is delivered on time by the yard. Twelve weeks is an estimate. Yards overrun.

**Net assessment**

TARNSIDE is simpler to execute, cheaper in the short term, retains the full master rota, and carries no insurance uncertainty. Those are real strengths.

VELLACOTT recovers its additional outlay in fuel savings in five years, eliminates the single greatest operational risk to the business (total dependence on a charter for twelve weeks with no fallback), acquires an asset twenty-two years younger, and positions the company for the following decade without the hull liability that re-engining cannot cure. The masters and insurance gaps are both closeable before commitment.

The balance of the analysis favours VELLACOTT, provided the insurance quote is obtained promptly and the endorsement training is sequenced starting now.

---

READING
  The financial gap between the two courses is GBP 950,000 in TARNSIDE's favour, but the GBP 190,000 annual fuel saving closes it in five years, after which VELLACOTT generates a net return on the extra outlay indefinitely. The masters problem is real but bounded by a training programme that can be staggered through the winter before the summer season; the insurance gap is closeable within the Kittiwake valuation window; and the linkspan modification is infrastructure spend that unlocks the asset. Set against those manageable execution risks is TARNSIDE's unmanageable one: a single-vessel, year-round-licensed operator placing the entirety of its licensed service on a charter that is not yet contracted, with no fallback if that vessel is unavailable for any of its twelve weeks. The Brindlemere's hull age means re-engining buys time but does not reset the maintenance and survey clock; the Suilvenaig's 2017 hull does. On a five-year payback, a materially reduced operational risk profile, and a significantly better long-term asset, VELLACOTT is the stronger course.

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The £190,000 annual fuel saving retires the £950,000 additional outlay in five years, and that financial case is reinforced rather than undermined by the central risk of TARNSIDE: a single-vessel, year-round-licensed operator cannot afford twelve weeks in which its entire licensed service rests on a charter that remains uncontracted and has no fallback.
